newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech c.bank to change min reserve requirement.
newsitem.headline: Czech c.bank to change min reserve requirement.

text.p: The Czech National Bank (CNB) said it had decided to exclude proceeds from securities issues including mortgage bonds with maturities of five years or more from its minimum reserve requirements for banks.

The CNB said in a statement issued late on Tuesday that the change, effective December, had been made to stimulate long-term savings. It also said that it saw a favourable inflation outlook with money supply growth slowing down.

The decision was made by the CNB's ruling council. In June the CNB announced it would raise the minimum reserve requirement to 11.5 percent of primary deposits from 8.5 percent effective August as part of an effort to slow down the rate of money supply growth.

"The Banking Council of the CNB approved a decision which aims to stimulate long-term domestic savings," the CNB statement said. "Effective December 1996 primary sources collected by the banks from non-callable securities issues with maturities of five or more years will not be included in the base for calculation of minimum reserve requirements."

Referring to its restrictive measures announced in June, the CNB said: "The adopted measures and the existing deficit of the trade balance are contributing to a relatively rapid decrease in the pace of money supply growth.
"Monetary aggregates are developing in line with the expectations on which the CNB based its monetary programme for this year," it said.
"Through this, favourable conditions are being created for inflation developments in the following period," it said without specifying exactly what period it had in mind.
"From this point of view, the development of the crown exchange rate, which has strengthened and has remained above the central parity level for several months, is also positive," the CNB said.

The CNB's three-pronged attack on money supply growth announced on June 21 also included a rise in the discount rate to 10.5 percent from 9.5 percent, and a hike in the Lombard rate to 14.0 percent from 12.5.
The following day it also raised the repo rate to 12.4 percent from 11.8.
CNB data released earlier this month showed that growth in the key measure of money supply, M2, fell to a year-on-year rate of 13.2 percent in August from 17.6 percent in July.
This was the lowest rate of growth in more than a year. Dealers believe that the CNB has a target range for M2 of 14-17 percent growth for 1996.
The trade deficit has grown rapidly, hitting 100.9 billion crowns in the first eight months of this year compared with 59.5 billion in the same period last year.
Inflation has remained stubbornly high at 8.9 percent year-on-year in September compared with 8.6 percent in the same month last year.

The government originally had an inflation target of 8.0 percent for this calendar year but the Finance Ministry now sees the average annual rate at about nine percent, forecasting 8.6 percent in 1997.
